newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds close stronger, spreads at new lows.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds close stronger, spreads at new lows.

text.p: Canadian bonds closed stronger on Thursday, with long bond spreads falling to 11-year lows, amid foreign buying prompted by increasing recognition of Canada's positive fundamentals, analysts said.

"It's a continuation of that same story. A lot of investors have woken up to the potential for Canadian yields to trade through the U.S.," said Michael Gregory, an economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers.
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond fell C$0.30 to C$106.60 to yield 7.427 percent compared to the U.S. 30-year benchmark which fell 19/32 to yield 6.88 percent.
The spread between the benchmark bonds narrowed to 55 basis points from 62 basis points at Wednesday's close. The spread is now at its lowest point since 1985.

Canadian bonds have traded stronger since yesterday, when Finance Minister Paul Martin reported that Canada's budget deficit in 1995/96 was C$4.1 billion better than expected. Martin also forecast a 1998/99 deficit of C$9.0 billion or about 1.0 percent of gross domestic product, and said a broad-based tax cut now would be wrong.
The report boosted Canadian bonds and sent the Canadian dollar to its strongest point this year in overnight trading.
"Slowly but surely the attention has been there from the U.S. and overseas," said Gregory.

A stronger Canadian dollar has also boosted speculation that the Bank of Canada will cut Canadian interest rates as early as tomorrow. The Bank of Canada last cut rates on October 2, bringing the key bank rate down to 4.0 percent.
In other prices, the Government of Canada 7.0 percent of 2006 rose C$0.20 to C$101.74 to yield 6.758 percent. The U.S. 10-year benchmark fell 12/32 to yield 6.60 percent.
The spread between the two benchmark bonds dropped to 16 basis points from 23 basis points at Wednesday's close.
The spread between the bonds is also now at an 11-year low.
The three-month cash bill traded at 3.45 percent against the U.S. three-month bill at 5.15 percent.
